desc:
Encoding. A circular singly linked list with n nodes is given by two arrays. The nodes are numbered 0..n-1; node 0 is the head, vals[i] is the value stored in node i and succ[i] is the number of the node after node i, and the last node links back to the head, so no node has -1. The node numbers say nothing about the order in the list: follow succ to find it.

Starting at any node and following succ for L nodes (with 1 ≤ L ≤ n) reads an arc of L values. An arc is a palindrome if its values read the same from the first to the last as from the last to the first. The arc may cross the place where node 0 is, i.e. wrap around the circle. Return the largest L for which some arc of L nodes is a palindrome.

Example: vals = [1,2,3,2], succ = [1,2,3,0] is the circle 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 2 -> (back to 1). The arc 2, 3, 2 has length 3, and the arc of length 4 reads 1,2,3,2 (or a rotation of it), which is not a palindrome. Also the arc 2, 1, 2 (starting at the last node and wrapping around) is a palindrome of length 3. The answer is 3.
constraints: Starting at node 0 and following succ visits every node once and returns to node 0
hints: First read the circle once into an array of n values. Checking all arcs (start, length) is cubic; expanding around every centre is quadratic. Both are too slow for n = 3,500 in the worst case (all values equal).
To handle arcs that wrap around, write the values twice in a row: every arc of the circle with length at most n is a substring of this array of length 2n.

Run Manacher's algorithm on the doubled array to get the longest palindrome around every centre, and cap each one at n (a palindrome around a centre stays a palindrome when you cut equal amounts from both ends, so you can shorten it to the largest allowed length of the same parity).
editorial: Read the circle into an array a of length n by following succ from node 0, then form s = a + a. An arc of L ≤ n nodes that starts at position i is the substring s[i .. i+L-1], and conversely every substring of s with length at most n is an arc. So the problem is the longest palindromic substring of s whose length does not exceed n.

Manacher's algorithm computes, for each of the 2n odd centres and 2n even centres, the radius of the longest palindrome, in O(n) total. A palindrome around a centre can be shortened symmetrically, so for an odd centre the best allowed length is min(2*r - 1, n or n - 1), taking n if n is odd and n - 1 otherwise; for an even centre it is min(2*r, n or n - 1) with n if n is even. The answer is the maximum over all centres.

The array copy and the Manacher arrays take O(n) memory and the whole algorithm is O(n) time. A simpler expand-around-the-centre solution is O(n<sup>2</sup>) and also works for the smaller tests but is too slow when many values are equal.
solution:
def longestPalindromicArc(vals, succ):
    n = len(vals)
    a = []
    cur = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        a.append(vals[cur])
        cur = succ[cur]
    s = a + a
    m = 2 * n
    d1 = [0] * m
    l, r = 0, -1
    for i in range(m):
        k = 1 if i > r else min(d1[l + r - i], r - i + 1)
        while i - k >= 0 and i + k < m and s[i - k] == s[i + k]:
            k += 1
        d1[i] = k
        if i + k - 1 > r:
            l, r = i - k + 1, i + k - 1
    d2 = [0] * m
    l, r = 0, -1
    for i in range(m):
        k = 0 if i > r else min(d2[l + r - i + 1], r - i + 1)
        while i + k < m and i - k - 1 >= 0 and s[i + k] == s[i - k - 1]:
            k += 1
        d2[i] = k
        if i + k - 1 > r:
            l, r = i - k, i + k - 1
    cap_odd = n if n % 2 == 1 else n - 1
    cap_even = n if n % 2 == 0 else n - 1
    best = 1
    for i in range(m):
        best = max(best, min(2 * d1[i] - 1, cap_odd), min(2 * d2[i], cap_even))
    return best
